title: Longest-example memory for automatic learning
formal: For every automatic language family learnable in the limit from positive texts by an automatic learner with unrestricted memory, does there exist an automatic learner for that family with memory length at most the length of the longest nonpause example seen so far plus a fixed constant?
definitions:
Fix finite data and index alphabets. The convolution of a finite tuple of strings is obtained by aligning their left ends and padding shorter strings on the right with a fresh symbol. A relation is automatic if a finite automaton recognizes its convolutions. An automatic language family has a regular index set I and an automatic membership relation {(i,x): x in L_i}. A learner may use any automatic hypothesis family {H_j:j in J} that includes every target language; duplicates, automatic recodings and hypotheses outside the target family are permitted.

A text for L is any infinite sequence of strings or a pause symbol # whose nonpause content is exactly L. Repetition and arbitrary ordering are allowed. A learner has a fixed initial memory and a total update map (m,x) to (m-prime,h-prime) with automatic graph, where memory is a string over a fixed finite alphabet, x is the next datum or pause and h-prime is a hypothesis index or the special no-conjecture symbol ?. Only m-prime is available at the next round; the output is not separate free storage. Success means that on every text for every target language, outputs eventually equal one fixed index j with H_j=L. Infinitely changing synonymous indices do not count as convergence. No negative counterexamples, queries about past data or extra tapes are available. Finite control is part of the fixed automaton. Bounds below hold on every finite data history, using maximum zero when no nonpause example has appeared.

Unrestricted memory means that no length bound is imposed beyond what the automatic transition can produce. For the bounded learner a constant c may depend on the family and learner, but not on the text or round. After any finite history sigma, its stored string m must satisfy |m|≤max{|x|:x is a nonpause datum in sigma}+c. The old and new learners may use different automatic hypothesis spaces and finite memory alphabets. Existence of the replacement learner is asked, not a uniform algorithm for converting learner descriptions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication with the allowed hypothesis recodings, or an automatic family learned with unrestricted memory but by no longest-example-bounded automatic learner. A counterexample requiring fixed rigid hypothesis indices does not suffice.
context:
The positive-text memory question is explicitly distinguished from learning with negative counterexamples, where extra feedback changes what can be learned.

The later transducer paper again notes the unresolved automatic-memory question; its stronger transduced model is distinct.
why: This asks whether extra memory genuinely increases the power of finite-state-style learning.

import_provenance.original_title: Does extra automatic memory beyond the longest example help learning?
import_provenance.original_statement: If an automatic family of languages is identifiable in the limit from positive examples by an automatic learner with unrestricted memory, must it also be learnable when its memory length is bounded by the longest example seen, up to an additive constant? The learner must succeed on every text enumerating the target language; equivalent automatic hypothesis codings may be chosen.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: This is the positive-data-only model. With arbitrary negative counterexamples, longest-example-sized memory is already sufficient for every automatic family.

sentences: An automatic learner receives every positive example eventually, in arbitrary order.
Its update relation is recognized by a finite automaton on synchronized strings.
The target bounds retained memory by the longest example plus a constant.
Hypothesis spaces may be automatically recoded, but hypotheses must eventually stabilize syntactically.
Negative feedback and stronger transducer models are excluded.
